The paper introduces SSRB, a large-scale benchmark for evaluating natural language querying over heterogeneous semi-structured data. The benchmark contains 14M semi-structured objects across 99 schemas and 6 domains, with 8,485 test queries combining exact matching and fuzzy semantic conditions. The authors demonstrate through systematic evaluations that dense retrievers achieve reasonable but limited performance, while fine-tuned models show improvements. The work highlights the challenges of semi-structured retrieval and provides a valuable resource for advancing research in this area.

In summary, this paper presents a well-motivated, large-scale, and valuable benchmark for natural language retrieval over semi-structured data. While some minor limitations remain, the contribution is significant, and the rebuttal effectively addressed reviewer concerns. Overall, we recommend acceptance of the paper.

As we approach the end of the discussion phase, we would like to express our sincere gratitude for your time, effort, and insightful comments on our paper.
In our work, we focus on evaluating the potential of dense retrieval in semi-structured data querying. We contribute a multi-domain semi-structured data retrieval benchmark via LLM data synthesis, along with test queries that combine both exact and fuzzy matching condition. We test representative dense retrievers and provide further analysis, showing that dense retrieval could achieve acceptable performance, yet they still lack precise understanding of matching constraints.

We sincerely appreciate the unanimous recognition of reviewers.
During the rebuttal process, we have strived to address the concerns in review, and have provided corresponding clarifications and discussions as suggested. And we believe that these concerns do not affect the core dataset contributions of the paper, but rather represent opportunities for further improvements of experiments.

All clarifications, revisions, and supplementary experiments during the discussion phase will be updated into the paper.

Best regards,

Thank you for having a discussion!

---

Regarding the relatively low scores on SSRB (e.g., R@20 < 25%), beyond the task difficulty, we believe this could be partially attributed to the strictness of the evaluation metrics themselves. Specifically, the metrics we selected—Recall@20 and nDCG@10—are quite strict. Recall@20 measures the ratio of relevant documents retrieved in the top 20 results to the total number of relevant documents. When k is small, the metric inherently yields lower scores. In fact, when we increase k to 100, the top-100 results naturally have more chances to include more relevant documents, and the recall scores improves, as the results in table below.

|     Marco Avg.    | R@20  | R@100 |
| ----------------- | ----- | ----- |
| bm25              |  2.01 |  5.79 |
| instructor        |  4.06 | 10.21 |
| BGE-large-v1.5    |  3.99 | 10.06 |
| Jina-v3           |  5.85 | 14.40 |
| Nomic-v2          |  6.06 | 13.79 |
| Drama-1B          | 14.42 | 34.09 |
| GTE-Qwen2-7B      | 13.66 | 32.55 |
| E5-mistral-7b     | 14.66 | 34.08 |
| GritLM-7b         | 13.65 | 30.96 |
| NV-Embed-v2       | 14.52 | 31.85 |
| Fine-tuned        |       |       |
| Qwen2.5_0.5b      | 22.70 | 54.46 |
| Qwen2.5_1.5b      | 24.17 | 54.67 |

For schema misalignment, when comparing the in-schema retrieval results in Table 3 with the cross-schema retrieval results in Table 4, we observe only a slight performance drop across all models. This suggests that the models are minimally affected by the mixing of content from different schemas. In other words, they exhibit a certain degree of schema structure awareness and are capable of distinguishing which schema a given query corresponds to.

For domain differences, we observe that models tend to achieve higher scores in domains such as Academic and HR, where each query typically has more associated positives (20.12 and 15.15 compare to the SSRB average 14.33). This increases the likelihood of retrieving relevant documents compared to domains with fewer positives per query. We take the scores of Nomic-v2 as instance, for Academic and HR, the R@20 scores are 7.86 and 7.31, which are higher than the average score 6.06.
And we will further refine this analysis by re-tagging the types of filtering conditions.

---

rebuttal.value:
> 1. The benchmark is entirely constructed using LLMs, from schema design to query generation and annotation. Although the authors vary generation configurations, the scale of 70k triplets per schema without any real-world or human-authored data raises concerns about the diversity and generalizability of the dataset.

We agree with this. Due to the sensitivity of data in certain domains and the lack of publicly available real-world corpora, we adopted an LLM-based generation strategy while grounding the design in practical scenarios.

This work can be viewed as a further step in the line of research on synthetic data for information retrieval, extending beyond query and relevance label generation to also include documents. We acknowledge the limitations of relying solely on LLM-generated data and are actively working on expanding the dataset with more real-world and human-authored sources.

---

> 2. The motivation for using a triplet generation approach (<query, positive, negative>) is not clearly explained. It is also unclear what benefits this strategy offers compared to alternatives. Furthermore, in the test set annotation, why do the authors retrieve candidates from all documents instead of selecting positives directly from the known positive set for each query?

Thank you for the question. We adopt the triplet generation approach because it has been widely validated as an effective method in retrieval [1]. Compared to other strategies, it ensures better alignment and consistency between the generated query and documents, as well as more meaningful negative samples, since all components are generated within the same semantic context.

Regarding the test set annotation, we retrieve candidates from the entire corpus rather than only positive in triplet because: each triplet is generated independently, so documents from one triplet may also satisfy the query conditions of another triplet. These cross-triplet relevance could be false negatives if they are not selected, this is a common issue in retrieval benchmarks. To mitigate this and improve evaluation reliability, we perform an additional round of positive selection from the full corpus and annotate their relevance.

[1] Improving Text Embeddings with Large Language Models. ACL 2024

---

> 3. Given that state-of-the-art retrievers still underperform on SSRB (e.g., R@20 < 25%), the paper lacks a deeper analysis of the underlying causes—such as the influence of filtering condition types, schema misalignment, or domain differences.

We agree that a deeper analysis is necessary to understand the performance. For example, across domains, we observe that models tend to achieve higher scores in domains such as Academic and HR, where each query typically has more associated positives. This increases the likelihood of retrieving relevant documents compared to domains with fewer positives per query. In addition, we have conducted some preliminary analysis of filtering conditions (see line 248), showing that queries with more conditions tend to yield more accurate retrieval results. We will further refine this analysis by re-tagging the types of filtering conditions. In summary, we will expand the discussion to better understand the performance.

---

> Consider including examples of failure cases or retrieval mismatches.

Thank you for this valuable suggestion. We are identifying representative failure cases and will include them in the paper. We will also showcase a few examples on the rebuttal page as soon as possible. Sorry for some technical resons we need to rerun retrieval embeddings. 

---

> Some writing errors: the citation to Section 3 in the Introduction lacks the proper symbol; the full term for "IR" is not given at its first mention; and “representative” is misspelled as “represnetative” in Section 3.2 and Figure 2.

Thank you, will proofread the text.

---

We greatly appreciate your thoughtful comments and valuable feedback.

If you have any additional questions or concerns, we welcome further discussion.

If our responses have addressed your concerns, we respectfully invite you to consider increasing your rating.

rebuttal.value:
> 1. The paper could benefit from a deeper discussion on how this benchmark differs from other retrieval tasks (e.g., passage retrieval, table QA, knowledge base QA), in order to better justify the motivation and task formulation.

Thank you for this insightful suggestion. We will include a detailed discussion.

Briefly, our task differs from traditional passage retrieval in two main ways: (1) our corpus consists of semi-structured data, whereas passage retrieval typically operates over unstructured text; and (2) our queries often contain multiple conditions that may require semantic reasoning, which is less common in standard passage retrieval settings.

In contrast to QA tasks, our retrieval task focuses solely on identifying documents that are relevant to a given query, without generating or extracting an explicit answer from the documents—i.e., there is no answer component involved.

We will elaborate on these differences and cite relevant related work in the paper.

---

> 2. The human annotation process is not sufficiently detailed. Key aspects such as annotation criteria, core settings, and thresholds for quality control should be explicitly described to enhance transparency.

Thank you for pointing this out. We apologize for the lack of clarity and will include more details. Currently, the annotation criteria and core settings are described in Section 1.2 of the Supplementary Material. We will make this reference more prominent in the main paper. Additionally, we will explicitly state that the threshold for batch quality control was set at 95%.

---

> 3. The dataset spans multiple domains and schemas, but the paper lacks analysis on how imbalanced distributions across domains or schema variations might affect model training and evaluation.

Thank you for the comment. We agree that a more comprehensive analysis is important. As we arr the early-stage work of this task, our current experiments adopt a uniform sampling across domains. We will include analysis about the imbalance issue.

---

> 4. The paper should further explain the mechanism for filtering LLM-generated data, particularly with respect to ensuring diversity, quality, and privacy preservation. Clarifying how low-quality or privacy-sensitive content is detected and removed would improve trust in the dataset.

Thank you for raising this important point. We will provide a more detailed description in the revised paper. Briefly, to ensure quality, we design specific prompts (Figure 8) to guide the generation and selection of high-quality data pairs for evaluation. However, we acknowledge that we did not sufficiently consider potential privacy issues. While all data is LLM-generated, it is possible that the model may reproduce sensitive information memorized during pretraining. We will conduct PII (Personally Identifiable Information) detection.

---

We greatly appreciate your thoughtful comments and valuable feedback.

If you have any additional questions or concerns, we welcome further discussion.

If our responses have addressed your concerns, we respectfully invite you to consider increasing your rating.

Thank you for helping us improve this work.

> ● The released code does not include the data generation pipeline.

Sorry for that, We generated the data using simple code by the vLLM engine with the prompts shown in the paper. We'll include the code for this part in the code repo.

---

> ● A non-negligible portion of the data may have incorrect labels, and it could be better with experiments about how such noise impacts trainable retrievers.

We appreciate and agree this valuable suggestion. Our current work mainly focuses on establishing the evaluation benchmark, so we have indeed conducted limited experiments on the training data side. We will include more experiments about noises. 

---

> ● Since all data is generated in a similar manner, many potential corner cases may not be well covered.

We agree with that and will explore more diverse data generation strategies in future.

---

> Figure 1: ● there may need some description. I’m confused about query to doc 1/2 and retriever to doc 1/2.

Sorry for the confusion, and thank you for pointing this out. In Figure 1, the “query to doc” arrows indicate that the same natural language query is used to search for documents. The “retriever to doc” arrows show that different types of retrieval tools return these documents as results. We’ll revise the figure and add a clearer description.

---

> Line 75–77: ● It would be helpful to include examples illustrating what the “missing structural fields” look like in practice.

Thank you for the helpful suggestion. We will add this. As a quick example, such as Figure 1, one of the documents might be missing the “weight” field ('weight' is null), which would affect how relevant the document is to the example query.

---

> Line 81–82: ● Since the ultimate goal is to retrieve the most relevant information, is it reasonable to include these methods in the evaluation?

Yes, and we also mentioned this point in Sec. 6 (Limitations). We are working on it and will include these methods.

---

> Line 108–110: ● Could different LLMs be used to generate schema variations? Relying on a single LLM might limit the diversity of schema structures.

Yes. However, to encourage variation even within a single LLM, we prompt it to generate multiple schema descriptions for a given domain in a single generation step. This global view allows the model to design a set of diverse schemas coherently across the domain, and thus cloud enhance schema diversity.

---

> Line 169–170: ● I’m not familiar with this rate, but a 10% difference seems quite substantial, especially considering this is a binary classification task.

Yes, from the task performance view, it is substantial. We consider the much lower time and financial cost by LLMs and suppose it is acceptable.

---

> Table 2: ● The Ref. Pos and Precision Neg values for Gemini and GPT are close to 50%, which may suggest poor performance or near-random predictions. Some explanation or interpretation would be helpful.

The values reflect the fact that LLMs tend to be very conservative when predicting positive cases. They only label an instance as positive when they are highly confident, which results in very high positive precision (Pred. Precision Pos. nearly 90%). However, this cautious behavior also leads to many missed positives, resulting in relatively low positive recall (Ref. Recall Pos. around 50–60%).

---

summary.value: This paper proposes SSRB, a benchmark for evaluating neural retrieval models on complex natural language queries over semi-structured data. summary.value: This work proposes a benchmark towards semi-structured data retrieving with complex natural language query, which leverages the LLM to construct 14M data with 8,485 test queries to support evaluation.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The work fills the gap in neutral retrieval over semi-structured data with complex natural language queries, an area that is underexplored yet crucial for real-world applications.

2. The paper provides a detailed data generation process, including clear templates and prompt strategies used, facilitating reproducibility.

3. A comprehensive evaluation of existing retrieval models is conducted on the proposed benchmark, revealing performance gaps and demonstrating the challenges posed by the dataset.

4. The paper is well-written, with informative figures and examples that enhance clarity and understanding of the dataset construction and experimental setup.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The paper could benefit from a deeper discussion on how this benchmark differs from other retrieval tasks (e.g., passage retrieval, table QA, knowledge base QA), in order to better justify the motivation and task formulation.

2. The human annotation process is not sufficiently detailed. Key aspects such as annotation criteria, core settings, and thresholds for quality control should be explicitly described to enhance transparency.

3. The dataset spans multiple domains and schemas, but the paper lacks analysis on how imbalanced distributions across domains or schema variations might affect model training and evaluation. 

4. The paper should further explain the mechanism for filtering LLM-generated data, particularly with respect to ensuring diversity, quality, and privacy preservation. Clarifying how low-quality or privacy-sensitive content is detected and removed would improve trust in the dataset.

summary.value: This paper presents the Semi-Structured Retrieval Benchmark, a large-scale benchmark for evaluating natural language querying over heterogeneous semi-structured data. SSRB contains 14M semi-structured objects and 8,485 test queries with diverse conditions, constructed through a LLM-based data synthesis pipeline. The paper presents extensive evaluations of dense retrievers, including both encoder-based and LLM-based methods, with detailed analysis across multiple query types and schema settings.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The paper tackles an increasingly relevant problem of querying heterogeneous semi-structured data via natural language, especially in the context of LLM agents and RAG systems.
2. The benchmark spans six application domains, and the dataset generation is well-structured with schema design, triplet synthesis, and LLM-based annotation.
3. The paper provides extensive evaluations across multiple retrievers and query configurations. The analysis includes both in-schema and cross-schema results.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The benchmark is entirely constructed using LLMs, from schema design to query generation and annotation. Although the authors vary generation configurations, the scale of 70k triplets per schema without any real-world or human-authored data raises concerns about the diversity and generalizability of the dataset.
2. The motivation for using a triplet generation approach (<query, positive, negative>) is not clearly explained. It is also unclear what benefits this strategy offers compared to alternatives. Furthermore, in the test set annotation, why do the authors retrieve candidates from all documents instead of selecting positives directly from the known positive set for each query?
3. Given that state-of-the-art retrievers still underperform on SSRB (e.g., R@20 < 25%), the paper lacks a deeper analysis of the underlying causes—such as the influence of filtering condition types, schema misalignment, or domain differences.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

ethical_comments.value: The use of synthetic data mitigates privacy concerns, and the authors acknowledge potential biases in LLM-generated content in Section 6 and Appendix A.

dataset_code_comments.value: The benchmark is well-packaged and accessible, making the benchmark usable for downstream research and training.

additional_feedback.value:
Consider including examples of failure cases or retrieval mismatches.

Some writing errors: the citation to Section 3 in the Introduction lacks the proper symbol; the full term for "IR" is not given at its first mention; and “representative” is misspelled as “represnetative” in Section 3.2 and Figure 2.

final_justification.value: After rebuttal and discussions, authors provide sufficient results and explanations to my concerns, so I decide to raise my score.

title.value: SSRB: Direct Natural Language Querying to Massive Heterogeneous Semi-Structured Data

abstract.value: Searching over semi-structured data with natural language (NL) queries has attracted sustained attention, enabling broader audiences to access information easily. As more applications, such as LLM agents and RAG systems, emerge to search and interact with semi-structured data, two major challenges have become evident: (1) the increasing diversity of domains and schema variations, making domain-customized solutions prohibitively costly; (2) the growing complexity of NL queries, which combine both exact field matching conditions and fuzzy semantic requirements, often involving multiple fields and implicit reasoning. These challenges make formal language querying or keyword-based search insufficient. In this work, we explore neural retrievers as a unified non-formal querying solution by directly index semi-structured collections and understand NL queries. We employ LLM-based automatic evaluation and build a large-scale semi-structured retrieval benchmark (SSRB) using LLM generation and filtering, containing 14M semi-structured objects from 99 different schemas across 6 domains, along with 8,485 test queries that combine both exact and fuzzy matching conditions. Our systematic evaluation of popular retrievers shows that current state-of-the-art models could achieve acceptable performance, yet they still lack precise understanding of matching constraints. While by in-domain training of dense retrievers, the performance can be significantly improved. We believe that our SSRB could serve as a valuable resource for future research in this area, and we hope to inspire further exploration of semi-structured retrieval with complex queries.
